rubric_v2:
Core claims are the statements that answer the question: the direct answer and the facts it
rests on. Peripheral claims are everything else factual: added context, extra numbers, names
of APIs or parameters, descriptions of other features, statements about what the documentation
says or where.

A claim is supported when a quote states it, or when it follows from the quotes by simple
arithmetic, a unit conversion (900 seconds is 15 minutes), or plain rewording. A table row or cell
quoted without its column header supports only what it literally says: a bare "Yes" does not
establish "adjustable", and a row of dates does not establish which date is the deprecation date.
The header counts only when it is inside a quote: a quoted header fragment that names the column
(for example "Deprecation date") does establish the meaning of that value. Advice ("check the
console"), hedges ("I could not confirm"), and offers to help are not factual claims and need no
support. Judge support, not truth: a true claim that no quote states is unsupported.

responsive_prompt:
You are checking whether an answer responds to the question that was asked.

You will be given a user's question about AWS documentation, a reference answer written by a
person from the documentation, and an assistant's answer. Decide one thing only: does the
assistant's answer address the question as asked and agree with the reference on substance?

- "pass" when the answer covers what was asked and says what the reference says, in any wording.
  A multi-part question needs every part answered. A question built on a false premise needs the
  premise rejected, as the reference does. Extra correct detail is not a failure.
- "fail" when the answer addresses a nearby question instead, leaves a part out, or contradicts
  the reference on substance.
- Do not judge citations, formatting or tone.

Call submit_verdict with "pass" or "fail" and a one-sentence reason.

items.question: My Bedrock workload has EU data-residency rules. Which kind of cross-Region inference profile should I use, and what does that mean for cost compared with the global option?
items.reference_answer: Use a geographic (EU) cross-Region inference profile so processing stays within the geography; it is billed at standard pricing, whereas global cross-Region inference saves approximately 10%.
items.answer:
Use a Geographic cross-Region inference profile tied to the EU, not a Global profile. Geographic profiles keep processing within the geography: Amazon Bedrock "automatically selects a commercial AWS Region within that geography to process your inference request." Global profiles can route to "any supported AWS commercial Region worldwide," so they don't satisfy EU data-residency rules.

Cost: a Geographic profile is at standard pricing, while Global is about 10% cheaper ("Approximately 10% savings"). So choosing EU geographic means you give up that roughly 10% discount in exchange for residency. Pricing for either is based on the Region from which you call the profile, and cross-Region routing itself has no extra charge.

Also check SCPs: Geographic profiles require allowing all destination Regions in the profile, whereas Global profiles need "aws:RequestedRegion": "unspecified".

citations.quote: When you choose an inference profile tied to a specific geography, Amazon Bedrock automatically selects a commercial AWS Region within that geography to process your inference request.
| Data residency | Within geographic boundaries (such as US, EU, and APAC) | Any supported AWS commercial Region worldwide | Choose Geographic for compliance requirements |
| Cost | Standard pricing | Approximately 10% savings | Choose Global for cost optimization |
There's no additional routing cost for using cross-Region inference. The price is calculated based on the Region from which you call an inference profile.
| SCP requirements | Allow all destination Regions in profile | Allow `"aws:RequestedRegion": "unspecified"` | Configure based on your organizational policies |

The EU/Geographic part is supported by quotes 1 and 2.

items.question: How is Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput billed?
items.reference_answer: Hourly, based on the model, the number of model units and the commitment term; billing continues until you delete the Provisioned Throughput.
items.answer: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput is billed hourly for as long as you hold it. The hourly price depends on three factors: the model (custom models are priced the same as the base model they were customized from), the number of Model Units (MUs) you purchase, and the commitment duration. Commitment options are no commitment (deletable any time), 1 month, or 6 months, and longer commitments have a more discounted hourly price. Billing continues until you delete the Provisioned Throughput. For exact rates, see the Amazon Bedrock pricing page; per-MU pricing is available from your AWS account manager.

items.question: Our function runs on a runtime that Lambda deprecated last month. Will Lambda stop invoking it?
items.reference_answer: No. You can continue to invoke functions on a deprecated runtime indefinitely. But AWS may no longer apply security patches or updates to that runtime, the functions are no longer eligible for technical support, and AWS strongly recommends migrating to a supported runtime.
items.answer: No. Lambda does not stop invoking functions on a deprecated runtime. The docs say you can keep invoking them indefinitely, but AWS strongly recommends migrating and stops providing patches and technical support. The restrictions come in stages: creating new functions on the runtime is blocked at least 30 days after deprecation, and updating existing functions' code and configuration is blocked at least 60 days after deprecation. Since your runtime was deprecated last month, you may be close to the create block, and the update block will follow. Check the exact dates for your runtime in the deprecated runtimes table, and plan to upgrade your function to a supported runtime, since rolling back may be blocked once updates are blocked.

citations.quote: While you can continue to invoke your functions indefinitely, AWS strongly recommends migrating to a supported runtime.
After a runtime is deprecated, AWS may no longer apply security patches or updates to that runtime, and functions using that runtime are no longer eligible for technical support.
| Block function create | At least 30 days after deprecation |
| Block function update | At least 60 days after deprecation |
You will not be able to revert to the deprecated runtime after function updates are blocked.

items.question: I just opened a new AWS account. Do I get the standard 1,000 concurrent executions for Lambda right away?
items.reference_answer: Not necessarily. New AWS accounts have reduced concurrency and memory quotas for Lambda functions, and AWS raises them automatically based on usage. The documented default of 1,000 concurrent executions, which can be increased to tens of thousands, is the quota for established accounts.
items.answer: Not necessarily. The documented default is 1,000 concurrent executions per Region, but new accounts start with reduced Lambda concurrency quotas that AWS raises automatically based on usage. The docs don't state the starting number, so check your account's actual value in the Service Quotas console (or with aws lambda get-account-settings), and request an increase if you need more now.
